query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, continuous, high‐temperature stable SiC coating on (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will suppress surface crack initiation and propagation, thereby enhancing the alloy’s mechanical integrity without compromising its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy in its as‐fabricated form exhibits a large caloric effect under applied-field/pressure-field operation but suffers from poor integrity and crack formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin (approximately 1–5 μm) SiC ceramic coating via chemical vapor deposition (CVD) onto the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: The coated and uncoated samples should be tested under identical conditions: cyclic applied-fields and pressure-fields at operating temperatures ranging from room temperature up to around 600 °C, with compressive loading rates similar to previous tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The SiC layer acts as a protective, high‐hardness reinforcement at the surface that inhibits crack nucleation and limits crack propagation, thereby improving overall integrity.
generation.mechanism: The high hardness and toughness of the SiC coating reduce stress concentrations and arrest microcrack growth at the surface without interfering with the intrinsic caloric active sites within the bulk alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the uncoated alloy (baseline with compressive strengths in the range of 152–218 MPa from epoxy composite routes), the coated material is expected to display a significant increase in compressive strength (targeting values appreciably higher than 218 MPa) and improved fracture resistance, while the magnitude of the caloric response remains essentially unaltered (within ±10%).
generation.baseline: The uncoated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which demonstrates excellent caloric performance but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and cracking.
generation.boundary: The intervention is intended to work under the same applied-field and pressure-field operational regimes as the baseline, at temperatures up to ~600 °C and under compressive strain rates typical for caloric actuator applications.
generation.uncertainty: While the expected enhancement in mechanical integrity is anticipated from the crack-arresting action of the SiC layer, the quantitative impact on both strength and caloric performance (and any potential minor changes in thermal transport properties) must be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38: one set with the SiC coating applied by CVD and one set uncoated (control). Subject both sets to identical cyclic caloric operation tests (applied-field/pressure-field cycling) and compressive strength measurements across the operating temperature range up to 600 °C.
measurements: Compressive yield strength and plastic strain under quasi-static and dynamic loading
Caloric response characteristics (magnitude of entropy and temperature changes induced by the applied fields)
Fracture toughness and crack propagation analysis (via microscopic imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SiC-coated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in compressive strength and crack resistance relative to the uncoated samples, or if the caloric response is degraded by more than approximately 10% relative to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Through evaluation and optimization of the primary dendritic phase, a unique non-equiatomic alloy, Mn17Fe21Co24Ni24Cu14, is derived. The combination and concentration of the constituents are distinctive and result in a mixing enthalpy of 0.49 kJ/mol, which resembles a regular solution. The alloy solidifies and recrystallizes into a single-phase FCC polycrystal. This unique non-equiatomic alloy can be utilized for fundamental studies by evaluating the equiatomic counterpart and emphasizing concepts related to composition-microstructure-property relations. It has the advantage of excluding σ-phase forming constituents. Together, the results emphasize the importance of enthalpic contributions within the scope of HEAs. Firstly, they demonstrate that even at high temperatures, a large mixing entropy does not always facilitate mixing of the constituent elements. This is evidenced by the duplex structure that remains partitioned after high-temperature annealing. Furthermore, the results demonstrate how the variation in cooling rates (from the melt) may significantly change the observed microstructure and phases.
